newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia-Germany ties get boost from Kohl's visit.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia-Germany ties get boost from Kohl's visit.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's just concluded visit to Indonesia is expected to boost German business interests there, businessmen said on Tuesday.

German businessmen in Jakarta said ties between the two countries were already excellent and, with Kohl's visit, Bonn is now poised to catch up on links with the fast-growing economies of Asia after initially missing the boat.

"Our relations are already very good. If you remember, Chancellor Kohl started the visit by fishing with President Suharto. The answer is there," Dieter Grosse, president director of the cosmetics company PT Wella Indonesia, told Reuters.
Grosse said Germany should maintain its key role in Indonesia's economy following Kohl's four-day visit, his second since German unification and fourth since becoming chancellor.
Kohl left Jakarta for the Philippines on Tuesday on the second leg of his Asian tour. He will visit Japan later.

Kohl told reporters on Monday his visit had been fruitful, even though his talks with Suharto touched on sensitive issues such as human rights, Indonesia's controversial national car project and unrest in East Timor.

During his stay, Kohl sought a meeting with Carlos Belo, the East Timor bishop who was co-winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize for his work in East Timor. But Belo said he didn't received an official invitation and the plans fell through.
Kohl's trip generated purchase orders worth some 600 million marks ($395 million) for German industries.
Contracts worth about 1.34 billion marks ($855 million) were signed on Monday, including the purchase orders and several joint-venture agreements.

Fritz Kleinsteuber, director of the Indonesian-German Economic Association in Jakarta, said German companies had earlier missed out on Southeast Asia's economic boom as they were preoccupied with unification and developments in eastern European countries.
"But now we are back. The strong German 'mittelstand' will help Indonesia because they are full of initiative," he said. Mittelstand is German for medium- and small-sized industries.
German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said experience gained in eastern Europe had provided German industry with a valuable lesson on how to restructure and modernise Indonesian industries.
"We offer what a growing market needs: investment and infrastructure goods in the broadest sense," Rexrodt said.
But both Kohl and Rexrodt were concerned over the declining numbers of Indonesian students in Germany, which they feared could harm German interests in Indonesia in the future.
One of Germany's strongest supporters in Indonesia is Jusuf Habibie, Indonesia's Research and Technology Minister, who studied at the Technical University in Aachen, Germany.
Habibie has retained close ties with Germany and Kohl.
But German businessmen denied that ties with Indonesia hinged on Habibie.
"I don't think so. We have many friends in Indonesia," Grosse of Wella said.
